entries.title: Tesla’s Make-or-Break Cybercab Had a Quiet Debut
entries.summary: An invite-only event in Austin, Texas, kept online fans in the dark for hours.
entries.content:
A Tesla launch event tends to cause a hoopla. Fans crowd into an event space; loud electronic beats are the warm up act. Finally, the star himself, the ringmaster of this electric circus, CEO Elon Musk, emerges to a roar. There are demos, powerful verbs, and sometimes, a “one more thing,” a last-minute surprise product unveiling. Fans and investors the world over look on—and post—online.

But for the road debut of the Cybercab, the driverless car that Tesla promises is not only the future of the company but also the global economy, an event in Austin came with no livestream. Invitees, many of them online Tesla influencers, were reportedly barred from posting about the event until hours after it started. And Musk wasn’t there at all.

It was a somewhat peculiar start for the Cybercab, a matte gold two-seater first introduced in 2024. Now 45 of the vehicles, which do not have steering wheels or pedals, are registered to operate on Tesla’s robotaxi network in Texas. On Thursday night, after the news embargo lifted, the online influencers who attended the event began to post sanguine reviews and clips from their first Cybercab rides.

The Cybercab is a make-or-break vehicle for Tesla. Musk and other executives have argued that investors should no longer think of the world’s most valuable carmaker as a carmaker. “Really, we should be thought of as an AI robotics company,” the CEO said last year. “If somebody doesn’t believe Tesla is going to solve autonomy, I think they should not be an investor in the company.” Musk has said that hitting its marks in those areas would make Tesla not only the most valuable company in the world, but worth upwards of three times more than Nvidia, today’s market leader.

But hitting Wall Street-ready milestones hasn’t been easy for Tesla’s autonomous vehicle program, at least so far. Musk said in 2013 that Teslas would do 90 percent of their miles autonomously within three years; that didn’t happen. He said that 1 million Tesla autonomous vehicles would be on the road by 2020. (Today, 420 Tesla robotaxis are registered in Texas.) He said that the Robotaxi network would reach 50 percent of the US population by 2026. Now Tesla needs a robotics win.

Driving a Win

Tesla’s robotaxi network officially launched in Austin in June of last year, with a handful of Model Y electrics. At the time, those cars came with human safety monitors in the front passenger seats, ready to intervene if the technology made mistakes. Since then, Tesla says that it’s taken human monitors out of many of its cars. The service is now picking up riders in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida, and has permits to operate in Arizona and Nevada. A ride-hail service in California must have a human driver behind the wheel of each “robotaxi” because Tesla does not have permits to operate driverlessly there.

Tesla executives say it will win the self-driving race because the cars depend on just inexpensive cameras to operate, making them much cheaper than those from competitors including Waymo and Zoox. (Those companies also use more expensive radar and lidar setups.)

Right now, though, the automaker feels behind. Tesla AI software head Ashok Elluswamy announced at Thursday’s event that the company’s vehicles had collectively traveled 1 million miles without humans behind the wheel. Waymo, which now operates in 14 US metros, said it reached 1 million driverless passenger miles in January 2023.

Tesla’s Cybercab vision is ambitious and wide-ranging. It plans to not only deploy the driverless vehicles on an Uber-like network, but to sell cars without driving controls directly to customers—and before the end of 2026, Musk posted months ago. (This scheme would likely require several major changes to the law.) It also plans to offer entrepreneurial Tesla fans the opportunity to operate their own fleets of Cybercabs. An "interest form” posted on Tesla’s website today allows people to indicate whether they're interested in Cybercab fleet vehicle purchasing.

Open Questions

It’s not clear how the Cybercabs will legally operate in public. Federal safety rules require that vehicles come with steering wheels and brake pedals, and also the systems that power those human driver-centric systems. Last month, the government granted its first-ever exemption for a purpose-built autonomous vehicle for the Amazon subsidiary Zoox, whose box-like vehicles don’t have human driving controls. The US federal government said this summer that it intends to fast track new rules that will make it easier for autonomous vehicles without those features to deploy in great numbers. But those rules aren’t finalized yet.

A spokesperson for the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told WIRED that Tesla has not filed an exemption request for the Cybercab. “NHTSA is in contact with Tesla and is evaluating the situation,” the spokesperson said. A Tesla executive has said that the company does not need to apply for an exemption.

And the Cybercab is just one part of Tesla’s projected future. Musk has said many times that the Optimus humanoid robot project “has the potential to be the biggest product of all time.” Eventually, he has projected, the robot will usher in an “age of abundance” that will render human labor moot. “The robots will actually make so many robots and AI that they will actually saturate all human needs,” Musk said earlier this year. “You won’t be able to even think of something to ask the robot for at a certain point. Like there would be such an abundance of goods and services.”

Questions remain about how exactly the robotaxi service works. Like other autonomous vehicle developers, Tesla says it has human remote operators ready to help or intervene if something goes wrong inside the car or on the road around it. Unlike other companies, Tesla allows remote operators to directly drive its cars from afar, at speeds up to 10 mph. These human operators have been involved in at least three minor robotaxi crashes, according to government data, including one in which a human drove an autonomous Model Y into a “hidden tree stump.” (Tesla reports that one has been hurt in these incidents.)

Still, Tesla executives seemed determined to have fun on Thursday, showing off the 22-inch screen in the center of the Cybercab’s console. If you don’t have to drive, why not watch TV? “You can choose to be entertained or choose to be productive,” engineering director Silvio Brugada told the crowd. “Anything you can possibly do as long as you have your seatbelt on.” The crowd didn’t quite roar, but it did “woo” suggestively.

entries.title: Wikipedia Workers Unionize for the First Time
entries.summary: More than 200 people in roles such as engineering, finance, and communications will now be represented by the Communications Workers of America.
entries.content:
More than 200 staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind the encyclopedia Wikipedia, have voted 158-14 to join the Communications Workers of America labor union. The US National Labor Relations Board counted ballots on Thursday.

Three Wikimedia employees tell WIRED they will now have a mechanism to challenge management as the organization faces growing competition from AI chatbots and a drop in volunteer editors. The 25-year-old, San Francisco-based foundation employs nearly 700 people across 39 countries, most of them working remotely. The contingent joining the union includes employees in functions such as software engineering, finance, communications.

Lauren de Lench, who has been a lead technical program manager at the Wikimedia Foundation since 2021, says she voted to unionize because she had seen too many colleagues decline to speak up during internal meetings out of fear of retaliation for raising issues or proposing far-out ideas.

“I want us to be loud and debate freely up and down the organizational chart because that’s how we move quickly, address challenges, and come up with the best collective solutions,” de Lench says.

The foundation said in an unsigned blog post on Thursday that it will “approach this next phase constructively, lawfully, and with care for the staff whose work makes it possible for us to serve people everywhere.”

Concerns about pay and benefits were not major motivators for the union drive, according to Wikimedia employees. Instead, they say, frustration over how the organization explained several hiring and firing decisions in the past year provided the final push the union needed to win the vote.

That included when the foundation chose to disband a team responsible for developing tools volunteer editors use to make additions to Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects, such as the image library known as Commons. In a separate move, management removed France from a list of approved hiring locations for product and technology roles.

In a sign of solidarity, some volunteer Wikipedia editors organized a campaign to improve entries about labor unions and related topics this month.

“I want to get to a place of mutual trust and there is a big gap,” de Lench says. “There are pockets within the foundation where it’s healthy, and I want everyone to have that relationship.”

In an organization-wide email seen by WIRED, Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan called unionization the start of a new chapter that she was “optimistic” about. “The concerns many of you shared about management practices, organizational planning, staff departures, and making facts clear and available matter as much as ever, and we will continue to work together to make meaningful improvements or all staff,” she wrote.

Growing Pains

Wikimedia workers have discussed unionizing off and on for a decade, but they had never gotten as far as holding an election before. Workers say momentum for the organizing effort began picking up after the foundation grew its workforce by hundreds of people during the Covid pandemic, introducing bureaucracy that left some rank-and-file employees feeling powerless.

“Management has had to walk back certain decisions,” says Nico Aramayo, a senior paralegal who joined the Wikimedia Foundation during the expansion phase. “Wouldn’t it be better if we could all have a seat at the table?”

The foundation is generally in a strong financial position, with an annual budget of more than $200 million and net assets of around $300 million and growing. But AI companies are increasingly scraping Wikipedia for information to train their models, driving up its server costs. Meanwhile, human traffic to Wikipedia articles is declining as more people rely on chatbots for information. Staff worry the trends could diminish interest in contributing to Wikipedia, damaging the quality of content.

As Aramayo and de Lench put it, Wikipedia needs to make a bold push to become more attractive than AI—and shaping that strategy shouldn’t be left to management alone.

“The importance of collaborating early and often, even if we don’t agree, is so crucial to moving forward on some of these bigger existential challenges,” de Lench says. “We need to embrace each other and the different skills and perspectives staff and volunteers bring to the table.”

Meehan, the former US ambassador to Chile under the Biden administration, joined in January. The one-time union member publicly told staff she encourages “dissent, good faith disagreement, and new ideas, as long as discussions are respectful.”

In the following months amid the personnel decisions questioned by workers, 70 percent of those eligible signed union cards and the group partnered up with CWA’s Local 9415, which represents staff at other nonprofits and telecommunications providers.

The foundation declined to voluntarily recognize the union, contending that a vote would be a more democratic process in line with its principles. But the foundation’s leaders stayed neutral through the voting process, workers say.

Wikimedia workers in the UK are also seeking to organize, and they hope to band together with the US group given that they generally share the same leadership, projects, and goals.

For the US union, the next step will be negotiating a collective bargaining agreement with their bosses. The foundation has hired Littler Mendelson, a prominent law firm known for combating labor groups, leaving workers to believe the company wants to put up a fight, says Aly Marino, a union member who is an attorney at the foundation. Dropping the firm, they say, could demonstrate Wikimedia is “committed to turning the page and working together.”

On Thursday, Meehan said management would work in “good faith” to reach a “timely agreement.”

Key provisions the union is expected to seek include requiring their employer to demonstrate just cause before firing someone. There are also some “pie in the sky” ideas that may be discussed, like shifting to a four-day work week, Aramayo says.

entries.title: 5 Best Video Doorbell Cameras (2026): Subscription-Free, Video, and More
entries.summary: Never miss a delivery. These WIRED-tested picks will help you keep tabs on your front door from anywhere.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

As people who receive a lot of packages, we at the WIRED Reviews team have a foolproof way of making sure an important delivery shows up: step into the shower. If you’re sitting at your desk with your shoes on, waiting and ready, I guarantee that every knock or ring will be from someone trying to sell you something or convert you to an obscure and weirdly expensive religion.

Even if you’re working in your backyard or hungover in bed, the best video doorbell can help you tell which knocks are worth lunging for and which ones can wait until next time. We've tested these smart doorbells for months, peering at Instacart deliveries and stray raccoons from the safety and comfort of our couches. The Nest Doorbell is our current favorite, but you'll find plenty of alternative picks that might work better for some folks.

Don’t see anything you need here? Check out our other guides, including the Best Indoor and Outdoor Security Cameras, the Best Subscription-Free Security Cameras, and the Best Personal Safety Devices and Alarms.

Updated September 2026: I added mentions for doorbells from Aqara and Ezviz, updated the Reolink Video Doorbell with my latest testing impressions, and updated prices.

Other Video Doorbells to Consider

I've tested several other video doorbells. These are the ones that narrowly missed out on a place above.

SwitchBot Smart Video Doorbell for $100: I don't love the design of this wide doorbell, but it does come with a wee display that you can use to view who’s there and answer. This could be handy for folks who don’t want to rely on a phone and it lets anyone in the house check who is calling. Video quality is decent, though the frame rate is limited to 15, and the display is low res. You can record locally, and there’s a subscription option if you want cloud storage. Sadly, I found the display was often slow to wake up, and sometimes I had trouble playing back recorded videos.

Aqara G400 Select for $100: This wired doorbell from Aqara is a mixed bag. It’s affordable, comes with a chime, and offers decent video quality (up to 2K). There’s local video storage if you insert a microSD card. It supports PoE or regular doorbell wiring, and has onboard motion and person detection. But it’s a big, chunky lump of plastic, night vision is below par, and you need a HomeGuardian subscription to unlock smarter AI detection (faces, animals, vehicles, and packages), rich notifications with screenshots, and AI video search. The subscription starts from $5 per month ($50 for a year) and also gives you 90-day cloud storage. Alternatively, you can use this doorbell with Apple HomeKit Secure Video (though it will limit the resolution), or with your own NVR or NAS, as it supports RTSP and ONVIF. It also works with other smart home options (Amazon, Google, and Samsung), but it lacks the Matter and Zigbee connectivity of the Aqara G410 above.

Philips Hue Secure Video Doorbell for $170: After a fiddly installation, you get a stylish doorbell offering sharp 2K resolution day or night and a wide view that takes in your whole porch. Notifications are swift and reliable, and you can sync up your Hue lights in interesting ways. But if you don’t already have a Philips Hue setup, I’d pick something from above instead. There’s no local storage option and you must buy a Smart Chime separately. Although you can get 24 hours of video for free, the false alerts will drive you mad. You must subscribe (from $40 a year) to get vital features, like people detection, activity zones, and back-to-back video recording.

Wyze Battery Video Doorbell for $66: Another solid budget option, you get decently sharp 1536 x 1536 resolution video with a 150-degree field of view from this doorbell. You can record locally on a microSD card and there’s good smart home connectivity, but you need a Wyze subscription, from $3 per month, to get person, package, pet, and vehicle detection, back-to-back video recording, and rich alerts (it’s not worth getting without this subscription). The indoor chime is sold separately, and if you want advanced features like facial recognition or descriptive alerts you have to pay more ($10 or $20 a month).

Logitech Circle View Doorbell for $200: As close as you can get to an Apple video doorbell, this compact hardwired doorbell boasts a 160-degree field of view with a 3:4 portrait aspect ratio that takes in your whole porch. Video is crisp and clear, in bright or low light, and the live feed is impressively quick to load. The notification system can tell the difference between animals, people, and vehicles, and will start to recognize familiar faces over time. It works directly through the Apple Home app, though there are pros and cons to Apple's HomeKit Secure Video. Ten days of encrypted videos are stored in your iCloud account (if you have a 50-gigabyte subscription or higher). Alerts come via Apple devices, but your regular chime will also sound when this doorbell is pressed. I love that live video pops up on the Apple Watch or Apple TV when someone rings the doorbell. The complete lack of support for Android or Alexa will turn some people off, and I encountered several issues with this doorbell cutting out and having to be rebooted at the fuse box.

Amazon Blink Doorbell for $60: One of the cheapest doorbells worth considering, (wait for one of Amazon’s frequent discounts to save even more) the Blink Video Doorbell only needs two AA batteries to run for months. But you need a subscription unless you buy with the Sync module (I recommend it). The Blink Basic subscription is $3 a month or $30 a year. Video quality is 1080p with a limited field of view (135 degrees horizontal and only 80 degrees vertical). The lack of HDR shows in mixed light, with bright areas blowing out and shaded areas losing detail. If you have a person at the door with light behind them, it can be tough to see their face. Notifications lacked images or video and were slightly slower than some of the competition, but they always came through. The two-way audio is passable.

Nest Doorbell (Battery) for $200: If you can’t hardwire your doorbell, the battery version of our top pick is still a great doorbell. I tested it alongside several competitors, and it consistently outperformed them. Alerts are swift, and notifications include animated previews that make it easy to decide whether you need to act. While the resolution isn't the sharpest (960 x 1280 pixels), and the field of view is 145 degrees, Google compensates with HDR video at up to 30 frames per second.

Doro Hemma Doorbell for £150: A simplified smart doorbell for seniors is a solid idea, and Swedish maker Doro gets plenty right with the Hemma. It is a battery-powered doorbell that’s easy to install and use, offering a 1440 x 1440-pixel resolution with a decent frame rate (30 fps), local recording via microSD card, and a plug-in ringer that gets loud enough to hear throughout the home. It worked reliably during testing, and the mobile app is deliberately straightforward, with a handy option to pass calls off to a trusted friend or family member (they’ll need the app too). The two-way audio works well, there’s a handy zoom function when you livestream, and there’s a siren to scare folks away. It is simplified, so there are no privacy zones or package alerts, and it may be too sensitive for busy front doors, though you can set it to alert just for doorbell rings. Battery life is decent, though the battery is not removable, so you need to take the doorbell off to charge or use a portable charger. Sadly, it is only available in the UK and Europe.

SimpliSafe Video Doorbell Pro for $170: If you’re looking for a solid security system, SimpliSafe is likely on your radar, and for folks with a SimpliSafe setup, the Video Doorbell Pro fits in neatly. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano found it sensitive at first, but, after an update, she says it worked nearly perfectly, sending swift alerts and offering a good, clear view of her porch. Footage maxes out at 1080p, but the camera supports HDR to banish glare and has a 162-degree field of view. It does have to be wired, and you need a subscription from $5 per month to record videos, but SimpliSafe also offers the option of professional monitoring (from $32 per month), which is a rarity for doorbells and might make sense if you have a complete security system with them.

TP-Link Tapo (D230S1) Smart Battery Video Doorbell for $109: For folks seeking a local storage option that doesn’t require a monthly fee, Tapo's smart video doorbell is worth a look. Notifications come through swiftly and include a still image; video quality is excellent, even at night, and the indoor hub takes a microSD card and doubles as a chime. On the downside, it is chunky, and the onboard AI (which is supposed to recognize people, pets, vehicles, and packages) is flaky.

Tough to Recommend

We didn't like every video doorbell we tested. These are the ones we don't recommend.

Ezviz EP8 Ultra: It took me several attempts to set up this doorbell. Despite following the exact same process each time, it only worked on the third try. Once I was able to set it up, I found it to be a feature-packed video doorbell offering dual cameras for a view of your front step and visitor, two batteries so you can switch in a charged one when it runs low (it can also work with doorbell wiring), onboard AI motion detection that includes facial recognition without a subscription, local video storage with 32 GB built in, and a plug-in chime. There’s also a light, color night vision, and AI characters (panda, raccoon, or husky) that will delight kids, but likely confuse delivery people. The video quality is decent, though the fixed frame rate (15 fps) is disappointing. It worked well when it worked, but I had real issues with it going offline. Even after I moved it closer to the router just to test, it regularly showed as offline in the app, and I couldn’t access the feed. It still came to life and rang the chime when I pressed the button. The EP8 Ultra is only available in the UK and Europe right now.

Ecobee Smart Doorbell Camera: Formerly known just for smart thermostats, Ecobee dips its toes into the smart-home ecosystem world with this 5K HD smart doorbell whose feed can be viewed in the Ecobee app or right on an Ecobee Premium model thermostat screen. One of its main selling points is the 175-degree field of view, which is a dramatic improvement over the older Ring camera it replaced on my porch. However, notifications for movement and people are alarmingly slow and inconsistent; the app interface is clunky; and it has thought my totally standard-looking doormat was a package every day for the two months I’ve been testing it, sending a notification any time someone comes to the door. Ecobee’s smart thermostats are still best in their class, but I’d skip this doorbell add-on. —Kat Merck

Imou Doorbell 2S Kit: Aside from being large and ugly, the Imou doorbell offers crisp video recording up to 2K with a 166-degree field of view, and it has a unique trick: the lens can rotate through 30 degrees to track subjects. The large size allows for a big battery, but this doorbell can also be hardwired. The kit includes a plug-in chime with a microSD card slot for local storage. Unfortunately, testing side by side with the Arlo, it failed to pick up some events. I also had major connection issues after changing my router, despite retaining the same network name and password. I had to reset the chime, which temporarily deleted the doorbell. It's only available in the UK.

Reolink Video Doorbell (Battery): We liked Reolink’s wired doorbell, listed above, so I was excited to try its first battery-powered model, but it was a disappointment. It offers up to 2K footage with a 1:1 aspect ratio that gives you a complete view of the porch, but you must turn HDR on in the settings, and it has a relatively low frame rate (15 fps). I like the option to go subscription-free, but it means putting a microSD card in the doorbell itself, and this is a relatively easy doorbell to remove. Reolink suggests up to five months of battery life, but my first review unit died after less than two and refused to recharge. Reolink sent me a replacement, which is performing better, but when it does run out, the rechargeable battery inside cannot be removed, so you have to take the doorbell off to recharge it. Factor in the slightly confusing app, relatively slow loading times, and connection glitches, and this is impossible to recommend.

Ezviz EP3x Pro: This is a far better-looking doorbell than Ezviz’s previous models, and it’s nice to see solar panels as an option for doorbells, though you will need a porch capable of catching some rays. The video quality is good, and you get a split view (like the Eufy above) that includes packages or waiting cats on your doorstep. The distortion correction works well, and there is optional color night vision with a built-in light, though it only works at very close range. I appreciate the 2FA, with fingerprint login, and 32 GB of onboard storage (cloud storage is an optional extra). Sadly, if you use the solar panel, you can’t connect to your wired chime. The lack of HDR is disappointing, human detection was a bit off (it frequently said I was a cat), and I had issues with alerts failing to come through on some Android phones. (Even after following Ezviz’s instructions, they never worked reliably on my Xiaomi 14 Ultra.) This model is not yet available in the US.

Botslab Video Doorbell 2 Pro: The flaky setup procedure required a couple of restarts, and physical installation was no better, as the screws supplied were so cheap that one of the heads broke off. The camera has a fisheye effect, but you can correct it with different views. I liked the VR mode, which provides a 180-degree view of your front porch. It comes with a handy plug-in chime, alerts seem reliable, there is an HDR option, and you can record locally (32 GB included) or in the cloud. You can also set a detection range, which could be handy for street-facing cameras. But the app is confusing, with an AI tab that lists various skills available for purchase. There is a login history and a limit of two devices signed in at once, but no 2FA, which makes this impossible to recommend. It is versatile but also relatively expensive.

Swann SwannBuddy Video Doorbell: This doorbell comes with a wireless battery-powered chime and the option of local storage, but the positives end there. The video quality is poor, the app is painfully slow to load and glitchy, and the doorbell frequently fails to register motion. I found the battery life disappointing. I must also question the decision to provide local storage via a microSD card inserted in the doorbell (the chime would make more sense and be more secure).

What Features Should I Look for in a Video Doorbell?

Here are a few factors that you might want to think about when shopping for a new video doorbell.

Resolution and HDR: The higher the resolution, the clearer the picture you get, but consider that higher-resolution video also requires more bandwidth to stream and takes up more storage space. If your front porch is in direct sunlight or strong shade, I strongly recommend opting for a video doorbell with HDR (high dynamic range) support, as it helps to prevent bright areas from appearing blown out or shadowy areas from being too dark to see. Sometimes it's called WDR (wide dynamic range).

Field of view and aspect ratio: If you want a head-to-toe view of the person at your front door, then think about the field of view and aspect ratio offered by your prospective pick. A wider field of view will take more in but can cause a fish-eye effect. Rather than a traditional landscape aspect ratio, you may prefer a square or portrait view to ensure you can see a visitor’s face and any packages that might be on your porch.

Local or cloud storage: If you don’t want to sign up for a subscription service and upload video clips to the cloud, ensure your chosen doorbell offers local storage. Some video doorbells have microSD card slots, while others record video to a hub device inside your home. You can expect to pay somewhere around $3 to $10 per month for 30 days of storage for a video doorbell.

Advanced features: The best doorbell cameras offer features like package detection and person recognition. These features can be handy for filtering alerts, so you only get useful notifications. Bear in mind that you may need a subscription to gain access to advanced features.

Security: A couple of things I recommend looking for are two-factor authentication (2FA) to ensure that someone with your username and password cannot log into your doorbell, and encryption to ensure that anyone accessing the manufacturer’s servers cannot see your Wi-Fi login details or watch uploaded videos.

Which Is Better, a Wired or Wireless Video Doorbell?

Smart doorbells require more power than traditional doorbells. If you opt for a wired video doorbell, you may need a new transformer, and you will likely want to hire an electrician for safe installation. The main advantages of wired doorbells are that you shouldn’t need to touch them again after installation, and they will ring your existing doorbell chime. Wired doorbells are usually a bit cheaper and slimmer than models with batteries, too.

Battery-powered smart doorbells are easy to install yourself and can be mounted wherever you like. The main downside is that you must remove and charge the battery every few weeks or months, which means some downtime unless you buy a spare battery to switch in. Remember also that your regular doorbell chime won’t work with a battery-powered smart doorbell, so you will probably need to buy a wireless chime device to plug in somewhere in your home, though you can also configure smart speakers to act as doorbell chimes.

Most battery-powered video doorbells can also be wired, which may be the best solution if you have concerns about power outages. Wired doorbells are generally faster to alert and more reliable than battery-powered doorbells.

How Well Do Video Doorbells Perform?

All smart doorbells need a strong Wi-Fi signal to perform well. Some come with hubs that double as Wi-Fi repeaters for a better connection. Remember that performance away from home when you access the video doorbell on your phone will be heavily impacted by the quality of your phone’s internet connection. Every video doorbell I've tested has a slight lag, but you should be able to see the live feed in close to real time and carry on a two-way conversation. While feeds should load within two to three seconds, occasional delays in loading the live feed are common, and I have yet to find a flawless doorbell. Video doorbells tend to load fastest in their native app.

What Is the Best Video Doorbell Brand?

While Google's Nest Doorbell is our top pick, it might not be the best video doorbell for you. If you already have a security camera system or plan on getting one, it makes a lot of sense to stick with the same brand for your doorbell. That way, you can access everything in the same app and get a single subscription if required. If you have a lot of smart home devices, check that the doorbell is compatible with your preferred ecosystem and voice assistant.

Why We Hesitate to Recommend Ring

Ring is reintroducing a policy to enable local law enforcement to request footage directly from Ring users, making its camera tough to recommend. We stopped recommending Ring a few years ago due to this policy, and that reasoning still stands. We also have concerns about its data collection (among other issues), so we have decided to stop testing Ring doorbells and cameras again.

How I Test Video Doorbells

I've been testing video doorbells for several years now. I install every video doorbell I test and use it for at least two weeks, but usually longer, as our main doorbell. I check the responsiveness when at home and away, test all the features in the app, and explore the smart home integration options. After the initial test, I install the doorbell alongside other doorbells (usually at least our top pick) and directly compare the response time and accuracy of alerts.

entries.title: Transplanted Pig Kidney Still Working After a Record-Setting 9 Months in a Patient
entries.summary: Gene-edited pig kidneys could offer a lifeline to patients stuck waiting for a human donor.
entries.content:
A woman has lived with a pig kidney for more than nine months without needing dialysis, a record-setting achievement.

The woman underwent the operation at Massachusetts General Hospital on November 22 last year. As of Thursday, the kidney has been functioning for 285 days, according to Cambridge, Massachusetts-based eGenesis, the biotech company that used Crispr gene editing to make the organ fit for human transplantation. Previously, the record for a person living with a transplanted pig kidney was 271 days, set by Tim Andrews.

Most people in need of a kidney transplant wait three to five years on average to receive one, though it can take longer depending on blood type and other factors. While they wait, patients often need dialysis, in which a person’s blood vessels are hooked up to a machine that removes excess fluid and waste from the bloodstream. Dialysis typically requires four-hour sessions three times a week and can damage blood vessels over time, making the procedure hard on the body.

Pig kidneys could offer an alternative until a human organ is available. Pig organs are similar in size and function to human organs and are being investigated as a way to ease the shortage of human donor organs. To make them more suitable for humans, scientists are genetically editing them to prevent immediate rejection and reduce the risk of pig viruses being passed on to transplant patients.

Patients' health gets worse the longer they're on dialysis, “and their odds of getting a human transplant aren't rising fast enough to meet their declining health,” says Mike Curtis, CEO of eGenesis. The company used Crispr to remove certain pig genes that could cause an immune response and add a handful of human genes.

“What we saw with Mr. Andrews was a radical improvement in his overall health while he was on the pig kidney versus if he had stayed on chronic dialysis,” Curtis says.

The woman who has crossed the nine-month mark is the fifth person to receive an eGenesis kidney through a special regulatory pathway known as expanded access. The Food and Drug Administration allows patients with serious or life-threatening conditions to gain access to experimental treatments when there are no good alternatives.

Andrews’ case shows that pig kidneys may provide a temporary solution. He received a pig kidney in January 2025 and had it removed in October last year after a period of decreasing kidney function. He returned to dialysis but received a human kidney transplant in January this year. A second person has also successfully received a human transplant after having a pig kidney for eight months, according to eGenesis.

Curtis says the company is learning more with each transplant. In a paper published on Thursday in The Lancet medical journal, the surgical team that performed the transplants details Andrews’ experience. They determined that Andrews’ pig kidney eventually failed due to thrombotic microangiopathy, which means tiny blood clots formed in the transplanted organ.

The team is using that information to adjust the immunosuppressant medications that pig kidney recipients receive and how frequently they need to take those drugs. People who receive human organ transplants also need to take immunosuppressive drugs to prevent their body from rejecting the transplanted organ. Organ rejection can happen at any time following a transplant, ranging from minutes after the surgery to many years later.

Kidneys are the most-needed organ, with more than 95,000 people waiting to receive one in the US. But due to a shortage of donor organs, fewer than 28,000 kidney transplants were performed in the US in 2025.

The FDA has given eGenesis the green light to conduct a more formal trial in up to 33 patients with kidney failure who are between 50 and 70 years old and on the wait list for a human kidney. That trial will not happen until 2027, but eGenesis plans to perform additional transplants under the expanded access pathway in the meantime. Their next goal is to get a transplanted pig kidney to function for a year.

entries.title: Nobody Is Saying Why OpenAI and Anthropic Had Outages Today
entries.summary: ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok all suffered outages at nearly the exact same time for reasons that remain murky.
entries.content:
Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI all experienced rare outages on Thursday morning, creating downtime for their corresponding AI chatbots. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, said on Thursday afternoon that the issues with Grok resulted from “an outage at our Memphis compute center this morning.”

The issues initially appeared to be linked because they coincided—perhaps the result of a shared third-party service provider—but neither OpenAI nor Anthropic cited an external source in comments to WIRED on Thursday. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. But the company said as part of its public comments on Thursday: “We’d also like to apologize to our impacted compute partners.” Anthropic and xAI announced a “compute partnership” with SpaceX in May.

OpenAI spokesperson Kathleen Chaykowski tells WIRED: “A routing error starting around 7:43 am PT on Thursday, September 3, made ChatGPT and Codex unavailable for some users across platforms. As of about 8:17 am PT on Thursday, a solution was successfully implemented and is continuing to be monitored.”

Anthropic declined to comment on the episode. The company began alerting about a “partial outage” at 6:23 am PT on Thursday that involved “elevated errors on requests to Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.” Shortly after, the company said it had “identified the cause” and that “a fix has been deployed.” The company marked the issue as resolved by 9:16 am PT. Claude Sonnet 5 seemed to briefly have similar issues shortly after 9 am PT.

xAI reported Grok outages across all of its platforms and services beginning at 6:30 am PT when the company posted “investigating outage” on its service status page. “Grok is experiencing issues. We are working on restoring service as quickly as possible,” the page said. At 10:05 am PT the episode was marked complete. “We have resolved the situation, and traffic is healthy again,” the company wrote.

There were scattered reports of a possible Google Gemini outage on Thursday morning as well, but the company did not confirm this or record any incidents on its service status dashboard. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment ahead of publication.

Typically, multiple outages in the same sector at the same time would point to a cloud provider, content delivery network, or other third-party vendor having issues affecting multiple customers. But OpenAI and Anthropic did not point to a potential shared cause, and major players in the internet infrastructure space—including Cloudflare, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure—did not report outages on Thursday.

entries.title: Prediction Market Betting Is Getting People Banned and Arrested
entries.summary: This week on Uncanny Valley, we dig into the latest prediction market buzz, Flock’s AI-powered police search tool, and how tech bros don’t know how to talk about “rouge” AI agents
entries.content:
Uncanny Valley is back! This week, senior writer Kate Knibbs joins Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger to discuss the two incidents that have been making noise in prediction markets: George Santos getting lifetime ban from Kalshi and a Google engineer’s Polymarket insider-trading case. Plus, reporters reverse-engineered Flock’s AI-powered person-search tool and spoke to experts about the accuracy of such technology, and the hosts unpack the online meltdown over how to talk about “rogue” AI agents.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Kate Knibbs on Bluesky at @knibbs. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Leah Feiger: Hey guys, so nice to be back after our two-week summer break.

Zoë Schiffer: Longer for me. It's so nice to see you guys.

Leah Feiger: I missed you.

Zoë Schiffer: I missed you.

Leah Feiger: Brian, don't worry. We missed you too.

Brian Barrett: I assumed that the you was for all of us.

Zoë Schiffer: It was the royal you.

Brian Barrett: But now that you've carved me out, that's telling. Thank you.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. This week we're discussing some recent high profile incidents in prediction markets. Former US representative George Santos was the first person to be given a lifetime ban from Kalshi, and a Google engineer was accused of insider trading at Polymarket. We'll get into why both of these cases show that there are still plenty of blurry rules when it comes to prediction markets.

Brian Barrett: We'll also check in on perhaps the most hated tech in the US at the moment, maybe a runner-up to data centers, Flock surveillance cameras. This week, WIRED reporters were able to recreate Flock's AI powered search tool, the same one that has a track record of being misused by police officers. We're going to break down how it works, and whether the backlash against Flock cameras might have reached its boiling point.

Zoë Schiffer: And because I simply cannot help myself, we will also be getting into why tech bros on X are melting down over how to discuss rogue AI agents and what happens when they jump their guardrails and coordinate attacks on other systems.

Leah Feiger: All right. Do you guys remember George Santos?

Brian Barrett: How could I forget?

Zoë Schiffer: Absolutely do, but wow, did not expect we would be talking about him again this soon, I have to say.

Leah Feiger: Former US representative expelled from Congress in 2023, accused of fraud and theft, and doing it with such a plum that the story just couldn't help but take national news by storm.

Brian Barrett: I want to be clear too. He wasn't just accused, he went to jail.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I was going to say very credibly accused.

Leah Feiger: Anyways, he's back in the headlines this week. On Monday we learned that Santos was hit with a lifetime ban from prediction market platform Kalshi, and a $71,000 fine, allegedly for trying to manipulate a bet on whether he'd show up to Trump's State of the Union. To tell us all the full details, we are joined by WIRED senior correspondent Kate Knibbs.

Kate Knibbs: Hi guys, how are you doing?

Leah Feiger: Kate, so happy that you're here. Can you take us through my favorite story of the week?

Kate Knibbs: I would love to tell you guys about this. And I will say, I feel similarly like Santos, yes, he does do crimes but he does them with such flare that it's hard to hate him.

Zoë Schiffer: It's a bad thing that's very fun to watch.

Kate Knibbs: Yes. So Santos, at this point when this all begins, he's already expelled from Congress, already gone to jail. He's out of jail, he's making Cameo videos for money, he's doing his thing. So, he posts that he will be attending the State of the Union. And then, while the State of the Union is going on, he posts that he's actually stuck at the airport and he's not attending it. And then he says, "FML." There was a market on Kalshi about whether Santos was going to attend the State of the Union, and someone made a bunch of money off of it. And Kalshi quickly figured out that it was him because Kalshi has know your customer requirements. His identity was not a secret to them, it was not hard for them to check and see that the person who made money was George Santos.

Leah Feiger: Awesome.

Kate Knibbs: And it's against their rules to place trades or wagers on events that you're a participant in. It's like market manipulation, insider trading, whatever. So even before this happened this week, the CFTC actually also knew about this because Kalshi told them, and they already fined him money for this specific incident. What happened this week was apparently there was this back and forth between Santos and Kalshi, and they fined him $71,000 and then weren't going to lifetime ban him. The same day that they announced the Santos thing, they announced a few other politicians who got in trouble for betting on themselves, and those politicians got much smaller fines and temporary bans.

Zoë Schiffer: Wait, do we know how much money he made on the market?

Kate Knibbs: I believe it was around 17 grand. I have to double check, but it was in the tens. They ended up enacting this ban basically because he was being a little bit of a prickly pear to work with and wasn't playing ball. So, this is Kalshi basically deciding that they hate George Santos, which is funny. He also immediately, he wouldn't give us comment, which was annoying, but he posted on X some kind of bitchy things about Kalshi. He immediately was like, "Let's see how long you guys last," kissy emoji. So, he doesn't seem super contrite, and I honestly don't even know if he's going to pay Kalshi. I asked them what they would do if he doesn't pay and they said that they would pursue legal action, and I am going to be following that because it will be interesting to see.

Zoë Schiffer: This is my big question. Does George Santos want to get away with these crimes, or is there something else going on here? Because it's one thing to participate in the market that you are literally a participant in in real life, but it's another to be blatantly posting about it in very obvious ways on social media.

Kate Knibbs: Well, if he did do it basically on purpose, he wouldn't be the first politician to do so. There's actually already a storied history of politicians doing insider trading on Kalshi, getting caught and then saying it was a bit. There's two other people who have already done this. Kyle Langford, who was caught this spring, and then this candidate, Mark Moran, who said that he did it on purpose as a sort of performance art piece against prediction markets.

Brian Barrett: This is my new get out of trouble card just in general, that I was just doing a bit. So, if I'm ever slow to put an edit back to you guys or anything like that, it's a bit. It's for my art.

Zoë Schiffer: And we totally get that.

Leah Feiger: I love it. I'm sorry, I think that there have just been so few rules and regulations, as you've reported, Kate, and there's just been a lot of gray areas that people have been tap dancing around that I kind of love an example where Kalshi had absolutely no choice other than to say, "Every single part of this was so wrong. Here are the facts from A to Z. This is it. This is the line in the sand." And I think that having examples like this is only good. So, that's where I'm coming from, I suppose.

Kate Knibbs: I get that. And you know what has been interesting? Because I'm so steeped in this prediction market world, sometimes I forget that other people don't know all of the arcane rules. And a lot of people have reached out to me about this story and been like, "Why is Kalshi allowed to fine him? That's weird. You don't get fined by FanDuel if you do something." And so, it's been an opportunity to explain to people it's because Kalshi is a federally regulated financial platform. It actually is imbued with the power to find people in the same way that the CBOE is. And that is something that most people didn't know, and now maybe they do, and we can thank George Santos.

Leah Feiger: Can we talk about Polymarket and the differences here? I referenced in the introduction the Google engineer who was arrested by US authorities back in May for alleged insider trading on Polymarket. Talk to me about this, Kate. How is this story different? How is it similar? How is Polymarket and Kalshi at this point different and similar?

Kate Knibbs: The Google engineer's case is different in a bunch of different ways. He made a lot more money, he made over a million dollars. So, the scale of it is quite impressive. He got arrested, Santos didn't get arrested for this. He's just gotten fined. He got arrested and he is pleading not guilty and is attempting to say that he's not guilty because he was actually just doing betting. And because he was just doing betting, the federal government has no grounds to attempt to try him under laws that pertain to commodities violations. Basically, the Google engineer was in Europe. He's a European living in Europe. When he made these trades using information that he learned because he was employed by Google, he knew who the most searched person of 2025 was going to be. He allegedly knew. And he's not, in the court filing so far, he's not trying to say, "I didn't do it." He's trying to say, "If I did it wouldn't be a crime as you're saying it is, because I was just doing international betting and what does that have to do with commodities law in the US? How was I insider trading? These aren't trades, they're just wagers." So, it's a really interesting case because he's basically allying himself with all of these state regulators that are currently battling the federal government and Kalshi and Polymarket over whether they're actually offering bets or trades, and it will be very interesting to see how it plays out. And the argument that he's making is also being made by the other person who was arrested for insider trading, the special forces operative. He's also making this argument. The two guys, I don't know if their lawyers are talking or what, but they're both coming out and saying, "Well, whether or not I did it, it doesn't really matter because this isn't trading, it's just gambling. And why are you trying to pretend that you can insider trade on a gambling platform?" And so, yeah.

Leah Feiger: Kate, thank you so much for joining us. I have no doubt that your reporting on how all of this continues, especially with the midterms, will be invaluable.

Brian Barrett: Thank you, Kate.

Kate Knibbs: Anytime.

Brian Barrett: OK, we're going to switch gears. We're going to talk about Flock cameras, which have been pretty reliably in the headlines the past few weeks, and usually not for great reasons. Lots of cases of police officers allegedly abusing the systems to track their colleagues, to track exes, and a lot of protests around them, a lot of people canceling their contracts with them, municipalities. This week, WIRED reporters Dhruv Mehrotra and Dell Cameron got their hands on the code behind how Flock's new AI-powered search tool works. This is actually some fun wizardry, they were able to take the code and recreate what it looks like. So, they're able to sort of interact with the Flock system in the same way that a police officer would. They don't have access to all of the backend stuff. And here's the thing, when you all think of Flock cameras, what do you think of them doing?

Leah Feiger: Surveillance.

Brian Barrett: But what kind? What specifically do Flock cameras look at?

Leah Feiger: License plates?

Brian Barrett: Yeah, they're license plate readers. Yes, this tool is not a license plate reader, it allows you to look up people. You can type in a general description. You can say, "Someone wearing scrubs, someone who has tattoos." You draw a little shape on a map, a little circle on a map, and the system will run a continuous automated search for a match across every camera inside of that circle.

Leah Feiger: That's so bad.

Brian Barrett: It's pretty bad. It's not great. And I think it's a capability that most people don't assume Flock has or offers, and it's a relatively new system, but we do know it has been deployed in some places already so it's out there. And not only that, there's not really a moderation framework in place. Flock recently announced some ways to make sure that people aren't abusing the license plate readers. This seems like so open-ended and such a chance to look for whoever you want, wherever you want using all of these cameras. It's really kind of stunning.

Zoë Schiffer: I want to dig in a little more on the it's really bad thing, because I mean, I think a lot of people are in agreement on that, but can you, Brian, just make the case for why this technology would exist? What is Flock's argument for why it could be good, and then why do you think it's bad?

Brian Barrett: So, I think the argument for why police officers like it is it's another tool to identify people who were near the scene of a crime, or suspicious looking people or whatever. So, I think it's just the more information, I would assume, that the more information you have as a police officer, the better you feel about the investigation. In terms of why it's bad, I think a few reasons. It is not a reliable tool necessarily. I think there's a lot about these sort of person recognition tools that aren't necessarily 100 percent you're going to get it right every time—

Zoë Schiffer: Like it can misidentify people.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, but even without that I think we already live in such a surveillance sort of state that we've become inured to it, but I don't think we should. I think the idea that anywhere you're walking you can be identified and brought into some sort of police probe because you happen to have tattoos, or happen to be wearing scrubs, or whatever other physical identifier feels like a pretty serious violation of your rights.

Zoë Schiffer: I will say it's been interesting talking to people about it because you really do get a lot of people who live in San Francisco being like, "Petty crime was a huge problem and now it's less of a problem," and that's really nice. And then there's a lot of people who are much more concerned about civil liberties violations.

Leah Feiger: Very specifically with the Flock cameras, the way that I've been talking about it with people is these cameras aren't operating individually. We're still relying on police forces to be using them and trolling their own databases, which then implies an inherent trust of the police state in addition to the surveillance state, which is already mired in a variety of reliability issues, accountability issues. So, the idea that a police officer in wherever, in San Francisco can be "fighting crime with Flock cameras" feels like incredibly surface level like, "OK, go for it, Batman." But when you're also like, "Well, which of these police officers have received reprimands from their bosses? Which of these are actually using these services to look up ex-girlfriends or family members?" The idea that this technology, which on its face doesn't have to be entirely negative, but is controlled by certain forces that could turn it to be so is very, very concerning to me.

Brian Barrett: It reminds me a lot of, or at least rhymes with geofence warrants, which for those who don't know, a geofence warrant is where law enforcement could go to Google and say, "Hey, I want to know everything about all the cell phone data, location data for anyone who was near a particular place during a particular time." This was, I think used, if I remember correctly, pretty extensively around the January 6 riots. They found a lot of people through these geofence warrants because they were able to say, "Hey, Google, who had a phone inside the Capitol at this time who was not a member of Congress?" The Supreme Court just a couple months ago ruled that those kind of geofence warrants do count as a search under the Fourth Amendment. So, you need a reasonable search requirement, it's a higher bar to actually conduct these things than there was because they were just going willy-nilly. Again, not a lawyer, but as a simple country tech editor, it does feel comparable in the sense that if you're going to be searching who is in a certain area at a certain time based only on physical characteristics or whatever else, there should be a higher bar for being able to do that. So, it is an unsettled question for sure, like what amount of surveillance is worth the return, but I does feel like people are leaning towards this world in which we've gone too far with Flock in a bipartisan way. We've had Florida just banned plate readers from state highways. Texas has stopped state funding for Flock cameras. I live in Alabama. Alabama, of all places, has started to say, "We need to take another look at these Flock cameras." They haven't done anything yet, but they're talking about it. And that's something to the point of like, "Yeah, we need to figure out where this lands." I think we're in that process right now, and it's landing on the side of maybe a little less Flock in everybody's lives.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm going to drag us to an even darker place on the internet. This past week, a blog post by the tech podcaster, Dwarkesh Patel, went viral on X. It had Silicon Valley elites up in arms. Basically, it was a summary of the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident earlier this summer. And to refresh everyone's memory, even though this feels like old news, this was when two OpenAI models went rogue and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face during a routine security test. Patel's way of framing the incident is what drew a lot of attention and ire online. He described the hack as part of this larger operation run by a group of AI agents, or as he called them, AI civilizations that rose and fell inside OpenAI during these training runs.

Leah Feiger: Civilizations.

Zoë Schiffer: I know, I know. Just stay with me.

Leah Feiger: Age of Empires, folks.

Zoë Schiffer: He dug into how the bots worked together to complete impossible tasks that they had been assigned. He nicknamed them based on their "behavior." One was called Alexander the Great, for example. He says there were points where you could see the bots sacrificing themselves for the good of the whole. All in all, the post had a ton of anthropomorphization. It reads like something that was written by a guy who loves to talk about the Peloponnesian War, which in fact, I feel like a lot of these tech podcasters do love to talk about that. But after the post came out, it was interesting. You really saw two takes, maybe three across X. On the one hand, you had people like Kevin Roose and Matthew Prince being like, "This is really scary and we should pay attention to this." And then on the other side, you had Tribhuvan Krishnan being like, "This post uses way too much anthropomorphic language." And then you had people like Chamath Palihapitiya who was like, "I think this whole thing is probably a psyop to shut down open source AI development." I made you guys read it, what did you think?

Brian Barrett: Well, I read this stuff also sometimes. So, I think we need to go to Leah for the pure unadulterated, "I am reading this only at gunpoint," take.

Leah Feiger: I thought it was a joke. I started reading it and I was like, "Is this Katie Weaver writing? Is this fan fiction?" I was sort of shocked at the idea of, to Krishnan's point, the anthropomorphization, say that five times fast, of these bots as a community. And perhaps the English language really doesn't have, despite our many decades of science fiction literature, shout out Tim Marchman who is currently listening and going like, "No, we have the language," but I don't know if we actually have the language to talk about what's happening here because they're not making communities. These are not synapses firing. This is very specific, something different. So, that was very odd for me. But also the idea of where this could go in the future was quite scary, because the idea that someone was not only recounting this, but was kind of pumped about it. It was spoken about lovingly, I felt. Is that incorrect?

Brian Barrett: Well, I don't know. I can't look into another man's heart, but I do think, Zoë, is it fair to say what struck me about this in some ways is A, two things. One, I think both can be true that it is over anthropomorphized. You said that so well earlier, Zoë, you made it look so easy. But then also, yes, it is scary that these bots acted this way. I think objectively it is sobering that these AI agents can do this. But also I feel like some of these people are trying to have it both ways. I think when AI is going to be your boon companion and your best friend and take over the world, it's fine to talk about them in human terms, but if you're talking negatively about them, "How dare you? They're just a bot, you're dramatizing it. Why are you being so ridiculous?" You know what I mean? I think it's really using language, as everyone has since beginning of time, but as is convenient for your case currently, how you talk about bots and AI agents really changes on what you want to get out of it.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I thought it was interesting because I feel like at this point we've all read a lot about this particular hack. And on one hand, purely on a literary level, I was like, "This thing is fun to read." He really did a good job being like, "Now, this battalion of bots did this crazy thing." On the other hand, it reminded me just as a writer how important it is to really think about the language we're using, because it did feel like rather than the focus of that article being what actually happened, the focus very much became how we talk about what happened. I also think it is concerning to see people like Chamath Palihapitiya, who is the host of the “All-In” podcast, but also has been involved to some degree, unofficially involved in the Trump administration and going to the White House and certain things, basically say that any level of investigation or media attention on a security incident is a psyop. I was just like, "Ooh, that seems like a really scary place to be going where you're so pro AI development that any publicizing of a security incident is actually proof that forces that want to slow down AI development are secretly seeding these messages places."

Brian Barrett: Yeah, I think that's a really good point. It kicked off a healthy debate, but not the right debate. And people are using it to distract from, I think, again, a really serious finding. I'm glad that it got more attention than it had been getting and that Dwarkesh really took the time to dig into it. But yeah, it's infighting over lexicography or whatever is not really where we need to be right now.

Leah Feiger: Coming up after the break, we're sharing our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Zoë Schiffer: OK guys, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is wired, whatever passe thing we're completely over is tired. Who wants to go first? Just kidding. I'm going to call on Brian. Brian, you're going first.

Brian Barrett: Thank you, Zoë. That's great, I win. So, my WIRED is AI job interviews when you go to interview for job and it's AI on the other end of it. This is an increasingly common thing. My WIRED is creating your own digital twin to do the interview for you on your end. Kate Taylor, who's a senior writer on our business desk, talked to a guy recently who, I found this amazing. He had talked to the same AI chatbot for different jobs five times because it was from a centralized recruiting agency. So he would apply to a job and it would be the same ... This AI chatbot called Riley, and you'd have to talk to Riley about why he was right for a job. Never heard from a human ever. So he said, "You know what? I'm just going to make my own digital twin of myself. They'll do the interview—"

Leah Feiger: Good stuff.

Brian Barrett: Did that a couple times. Then he made an AI chatbot that he thought was the idealized candidate and had that do an interview. None of them ever got called back either. I do recommend going to find cases around WIRED because we did publish video of this guy's chatbot talking to the interview chatbot, and it is delightful.

Zoë Schiffer: That's so great. OK, Leah, what about you?

Leah Feiger: My WIRED and TIRED this week is incredibly bad, and it's clear that I'm slightly phoning it in, but all I can think about right now, you guys, is the midterms are so close. That's my WIRED because I'm so excited.

Zoë Schiffer: You are so tired though. You are straight up so tired.

Leah Feiger: I'm so tired, but I'm wired because the midterms are pretty much here. Primary season was a slog, and it's done, and I'm just so excited for what's to come. My TIRED is some Democrats are starting to count their chickens before they hatch, and that is wild to see. Our wonderful senior correspondent and author of the Inner Loop newsletter for WIRED, Hugo Lowell, has a piece out all about how Democrats are already planning for subpoenas to fly once Democrats take control of the House, and what repercussions they could land on the administration should they not comply. And while that's all very lovely and good, the elections have not happened yet, and there is so much disarray within the Democratic Party at the moment in some very key states, I'm looking at you, Maine, I'm looking at you, Michigan, that I'm not ... I don't know. It's a little bit concerning to watch that happen from afar.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, I just have to say, I feel like if Democrats learned anything over the past eight years, it's to not count the chickens. Don't count the ... Just wait. Don't count them.

Brian Barrett: Don't count them.

Zoë Schiffer: Maybe even after they hatch—

Brian Barrett: Don't do it.

Zoë Schiffer: The chickens could be really old and tired, and that could be a whole thing. My WIRED is combining an AI agent with your savvy human friend to plan your life. Leah's dying right now as I say it. Hear me out. I'm going to Venice next week, humble brag, brag bag. Don't know a lot about it, asked Leah for recommendations. She gave me a bunch, I was so excited. Didn't want to book all of this myself because I had a very busy week. Tried out one of the buzzy AI assistants that is taking over Silicon Valley. That's one of the ones you just text and say, "Hey, can you do this thing?" Speaking of surveillance, you do have to give it access to a lot of stuff, so that's that. And thus, I'm not going to talk about which one I'm using lest my phone get hacked. However, it booked all of my reservations for me, and I did kind of have a moment where I was like, "This is sick." I just gave it the list and was like, "Based on where I'm going these days, can you make the reservations, lunch and dinner?" Done.

Leah Feiger: Wait, but how? These were mom and pop middle ... They have a phone number that they barely answered.

Zoë Schiffer: At times, it emailed them or WhatsApped them.

Leah Feiger: Oh …

Zoë Schiffer: I know.

Leah Feiger: ... my God. Wait, this is sort of transformational. Usually when we go places I make a list and give it to Rodrigo, and I'm like, "And now you have to spend the next five days figuring out between siesta and dinner when you're able to call."

Brian Barrett: So it's sort of like having a Rodrigo, but a digital twin.

Zoë Schiffer: Rodrigo's one of our most avid listeners. Hi, Rodrigo.

Leah Feiger: I'm actually really excited to hear how this goes.

Zoë Schiffer: If I show up to the restaurant and they're like, "We've never heard of you," that would be really funny. No, but I feel like, I mean, kind of like the surveillance conversation, it is this question of you need to give agents enough access to your systems in order for them to be really useful, but then we just don't have the right tools in place to stop them if they get very motivated from going rogue. That was the whole thing about the OpenAI incident is it gave them an impossible task and then they really tried to succeed. So yeah, I think that there are huge risks with these systems, but again, a lot of people in Silicon Valley are using them, me included apparently. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Marc Leyda is our San Francisco studio engineer. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

entries.title: GPT-6 Astra Is Here—and OpenAI Thinks It May Kick Off the AGI Era
entries.summary: OpenAI leaders think the company’s next generation model, which excels at computer use and coding, may mark a major milestone in AI development.
entries.content:
OpenAI announced Thursday the launch of its next generation AI model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company claims is state of the art at navigating computers and web browsers, writing software, and solving difficult math problems.

It plans to make GPT-6 Astra available to paid customers in the coming days, starting with a limited set of organizations, including enterprise clients in its Daybreak early access program, followed by ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise plan subscribers. OpenAI did not say whether GPT-6 Astra will be available to free users of ChatGPT.

In a press briefing with reporters, OpenAI executives made it clear that they feel very confident about the company’s latest AI model. President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he personally believes the world is now in the era of artificial general intelligence, or AI systems that are generally smarter than humans.

“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” Brockman told reporters. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."

OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Astra at a critical moment for the company. The ChatGPT maker is trying to rapidly advance its technology and boost sales ahead of a planned initial offering while simultaneously avoiding compromising on safety and security. OpenAI is also facing stiff competition from Anthropic, its most important rival, which is also working on an upcoming IPO.

In a blog post, OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming it can navigate computers and web browsers on behalf of humans far better than its predecessors. AI companies have historically struggled to make models that can reliably browse websites, fill out forms, and manipulate software tools quickly and accurately enough to replace humans. In tests, OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra was able to book DMV appointments, search for job listings, and apartment hunt faster than the average person could.

The company also claims GPT-6 Astra is also the most safe and aligned AI model OpenAI has ever released. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company is monitoring GPT-6 Astra’s chain-of-thought—the model’s internal scratchpad it uses to work through problems—to ensure it is deployed safely. However, Pachocki said that making sure advanced AI models don’t cause unintended harm is increasingly a challenge, and may present a bottleneck to further AI progress.

“We kind of take this visibility for granted, and we are seeing that as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging,” said Pachocki. “We think confidence in monitoring may constrain further development, because we would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We would withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.”

entries.title: OpenAI Cut Off a Billion-Dollar Customer to Avoid Elon Musk
entries.summary: OpenAI recently estimated its Cursor partnership would make more than $1 billion in revenue a year, WIRED has learned. It still walked away after Elon Musk’s SpaceX acquired the AI coding startup.
entries.content:
In a late-night blog post last Friday, OpenAI said it would wind down its partnership with Cursor, the startup behind one of the most popular AI coding tools on the market. The reason OpenAI gave for the decision is effectively that it can’t trust Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX recently acquired Cursor in a $60 billion deal.

In doing so, OpenAI walked away from one of its most important customers. Cursor has long paid OpenAI fees to offer the ChatGPT-maker’s models to developers using its AI coding editor. At the start of 2026, Cursor was one of OpenAI’s top five customers in terms of revenue, people familiar with the matter tell WIRED. By the spring of this year, OpenAI estimated Cursor would bring in more than $1 billion in annualized revenue for the ChatGPT maker, based on the partnership’s performance at that time, the people said.

The figures, which have not been previously reported, indicate the financial loss OpenAI is willing to take on to avoid doing business with Musk. OpenAI declined to comment. Representatives for SpaceX and Cursor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.

“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts,” said OpenAI in the blog post.

As OpenAI prepares to go public next year, it’s trying to show investors a more stable business—ideally one that doesn’t rely so heavily on the goodwill of Musk. OpenAI reportedly now generates more than $40 billion in annualized revenue, drawing on several different lines of business, including subscriptions, ads in ChatGPT, and selling access to its AI coding tool, Codex.

Losing a major customer like Cursor may not hurt OpenAI financially as much as it once would have, but it was certainly a difficult decision. The company acknowledged in its blog post that ending the partnership may damage its standing with developers—a community it has spent years carefully working to win over—by cutting off a major channel they use to access OpenAI’s models.

Michael Truell, Cursor’s founder and CEO, who is now leading teams at SpaceX, responded publicly to OpenAI’s announcement hours later on Friday in a post on X, claiming that the ChatGPT-maker’s models only “serve about 5% of Cursor user traffic.” The comment seemed designed to imply that OpenAI’s models weren’t very popular with developers using Cursor, and wouldn’t meaningfully affect its business.

OpenAI’s head of core products, Thibault Sottiaux, was quick to point out that token usage is “not a proxy for revenue nor value created,” and asked Truell to “share the math” behind the 5 percent number.

WIRED previously reported that Cursor leaders hoped to remain a platform for third-party AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic, even after the SpaceX acquisition. Some AI insiders considered that wishful thinking, assuming that Cursor and OpenAI’s breakup has long been a foregone conclusion. As OpenAI builds Codex into a large AI coding business, it increasingly finds itself competing with Cursor for customers. Nevertheless, the companies have operated relatively peacefully, as partners and competitors, for well over a year.

Evidently, that arrangement was no longer possible with Musk in control of Cursor. OpenAI may have determined that its Cursor partnership was not worth the risk that SpaceX might distill its best AI models. The company noted in its blog post that, earlier this year, Musk seemingly said that xAI—now a part of SpaceX—used OpenAI’s models to train its own. The apparent admission came during Musk’s deposition in his lawsuit against OpenAI, in which he claimed that Sam Altman and Greg Brockman had stolen a charity they created together roughly a decade ago. A federal jury dismissed the suit earlier this year.

OpenAI and Cursor have a long, complicated history of their own. OpenAI’s startup fund was one of the first investors in Cursor, participating in its 2023 seed round. At the time, the idea that a young startup could compete with Microsoft’s popular AI coding tool, GitHub Copilot, seemed like a pipe dream. But in the years since, Cursor’s popularity with developers became undeniable.

WIRED previously reported that OpenAI approached Cursor about an acquisition at one point, though the talks never reached an advanced stage. By the summer of 2025, Truell appeared prominently in OpenAI’s marketing materials for the launch of its long awaited GPT-5 AI model.

Cursor isn’t done with third-party AI models just yet. In the wake of OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown said his company would continue to make Claude models available in Cursor. I’m not sure that’s out of the goodness of their heart—Anthropic may have to play nice with Cursor because it depends on Musk’s SpaceX for $45 billion of data center capacity. Last year, Anthropic had no problem cutting off the AI coding startup called Windsurf when OpenAI was rumored to be acquiring it. (Windsurf was ultimately bought by another startup, Cognition.) At the time, Anthropic cofounder Jared Kaplan told me, “It would be odd for us to sell Claude to OpenAI.”

I guess it’s fine to sell Claude to SpaceX, though?
